compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 2022-12 edition. The 2021-Q1 edition README (same repo) says all runtimes were built from git in release mode, the wasm came from libsodium's dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench with LLVM 11.1.0 and wasm-opt -O4, identical wasm files for every runtime.
name: Wasmer (LLVM backend)
workload: Libsodium's built-in crypto benchmark suite (about 70 primitives such as AEAD, hashes, signatures, box) compiled once to WASI and run in each runtime, December 2022 edition, wasmer with its LLVM compiler backend.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean of per-benchmark time ratios over the 69 benchmarks present in both CSVs (derived from page data): wasmer-llvm is 0.872x the time of wasmtime (about 1.15x faster; faster on 54 of 69 benchmarks) and 0.747x the time of node/V8 (about 1.34x faster; faster on 60 of 69). The same data show wasmer-cranelift at 1.02x the wasmtime time (no gain) and wasmer-singlepass at 3.12x (slower).
license: MIT (repository); BUSL-1.1 for the LLVM and Singlepass compiler crates from Wasmer 6.0
tradeoffs: The LLVM backend compiles far slower than Cranelift and needs a matching LLVM install (LLVM 22 now); for startup-sensitive use the Cranelift or Singlepass backends are the practical choices. Wasmer is a runtime with its own WASIX layer, not a drop-in for the Wasmtime embedding API.
caveats: Ratios are derived by this agent from the raw per-benchmark CSVs (wasmer-llvm.csv, wasmtime.csv, node.csv) in the archived benchmark repo, geometric mean over 69 shared rows; the repo carries no 2022-12 README, so CPU model, runtime versions and flags for that edition are not stated. Compile time is not part of the measured numbers (LLVM compile is far slower). The 2021-Q1 README by the same author ranked WAVM ahead of wasmer-llvm and the author's 2026 post (blocked here, snippet only) reports Wasmtime ahead of Wasmer overall, so the win is specific to the LLVM backend and to this crypto-heavy workload. LICENCE WARNING: the repo root is MIT, but lib/compiler-llvm/LICENSE (and the singlepass crate) is Business Source License 1.1 for Wasmer LLVM 6.0.0 or later, with production use allowed only for Wasmer sponsors (change date four years after publication, change licence MPL-2.0); the December 2022 numbers were measured on the older MIT-era LLVM backend. Wasmer is itself a named baseline; this entry is evidence that its LLVM backend beats Wasmtime's default and V8 on steady-state throughput.

compiler_and_flags: StarlingMonkey built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DUSE_WASM_OPT=OFF -DWEVAL=ON; runtime is wasmtime serve (version not stated).
name: weval
baseline: generic SpiderMonkey (StarlingMonkey) JavaScript interpreter running on Wasmtime
workload: Octane benchmarks (Richards in the quoted PR) on SpiderMonkey compiled to Wasm and then partially evaluated by weval, run under 'wasmtime serve', versus the same interpreter without weval.
claimed_speedup: README: '3-5x speedups over the generic interpreter'. StarlingMonkey PR #91 quotes Richards score 676 with weval AOT versus 189 for the plain interpreter (about 3.6x, derived from page data). The PLDI 2025 paper's abstract (seen only as a search snippet) reports 2.17x average on SpiderMonkey and 1.84x on PUC-Rio Lua.
stars_or_usage: 149 stars; used by StarlingMonkey and ComponentizeJS for AOT JavaScript on Wasm
tradeoffs: Needs the interpreter source to be annotated with weval's intrinsics (include/weval.h) and a Wizer snapshot step in the build; the output is Wasm, so it still runs on any Wasm engine, but compile time and module size grow.
caveats: The baseline is the project's own un-wevaled interpreter, not a rival runtime, so the speedup says nothing about Wasmtime or V8 relative speed. The README gives a range without methodology; the PR does not state hardware or the Wasmtime version. The peer-reviewed paper (cfallin.org PDF, ACM DL) was blocked from this environment, so the 2.17x/1.84x averages are from a search snippet only and tier is held at C.

name: evm2 (alloy-rs)
workload: EVM bytecode execution; the README does not name the workloads. The repo's bench.yml runs interpreter and JIT benchmark shards under CodSpeed.
claimed_speedup: README: 'up to 2x faster than revm from a tighter interpreter, static dispatch tables, and cheaper instruction plumbing'.

'Up to' means best case. The gophersg/evm2 fork shows the same README text.

name: Guillotine (evmts)
baseline: REVM (Rust EVM interpreter) and Geth EVM
workload: evm-bench test cases (erc20-approval-transfer, erc20-mint, erc20-transfer, ten-thousand-hashes, snailtracer) timed with hyperfine per run.
claimed_speedup: README table, ms per run, Guillotine vs REVM vs Geth vs evmone: erc20-approval-transfer 1.59/1.67/3.65/1.56; erc20-mint 4.28/5.76/12.84/4.26; erc20-transfer 6.65/8.30/17.50/6.01; ten-thousand-hashes 2.46/3.31/9.36/2.90; snailtracer 26.41/39.01/86.02/27.15. So about 1.05x to 1.48x faster than REVM and 2.3x to 3.8x faster than Geth (derived from page data); on par with evmone (slower on 3 of 5 rows).
tradeoffs: Early-alpha Zig EVM with comptime-configurable features; the repo page reports about 48% of its own tests failing (mostly elliptic-curve precompiles) and says it is being refactored.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler flags or versions; the benchmark harness was moved out of the repo (the evmts/evm-benchmarks repo that replaced it shows REVM winning in its example output). The README states it is on par with evmone, not faster. Early alpha with failing tests, so the speed may omit work a conforming EVM must do.

name: Life (perlin-network)
workload: Three programs compiled to WebAssembly: 128-bit Pollard rho factoring, Snappy compression and recursive Fibonacci, timed end to end.
claimed_speedup: Raw results gist, real time: Pollard rho Life JIT 1.672 s, interpreter 2.178 s, wagon 4.349 s, wasmi 4.852 s; Snappy compress Life JIT 1.072 s, interpreter 2.977 s, wagon 5.443 s, wasmi 7.017 s; recursive Fibonacci Life JIT 3.898 s, interpreter 3.071 s, wagon 6.204 s, wasmi 5.811 s. So roughly 1.5x to 6.5x faster than wasmi with the JIT/AOT engine and 1.9x to 2.4x with the plain interpreter, and 1.6x to 5.1x faster than wagon with the JIT (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Pure-Go interpreter (no cgo) plus an experimental AOT/JIT engine that needs native code generation; implements WebAssembly MVP only (66 of 72 spec tests passed at the time) and has no WASI or modern proposals.
caveats: Numbers date from 2019 against the then-current wasmi (a much slower pre-register-machine design) and wagon, so they do not carry to wasmi 1.x/2.x, wasm3 or Wasmtime. No hardware, flags or versions are stated; the README only shows a chart image and links the gist. The repo was last committed in December 2019.

compiler_and_flags: Engine versions listed (wasmtime 45.0.1/46.0.1, wasmer 7.1.0/7.3.0, V8 15.1.42/15.2.20, wazero 1.12.0, wasm3, wasmi_cli 1.1.0, WAVM prerelease); Go toolchain and build flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (pinned to CPU 7) and Apple M4 Max
name: Wago
workload: A 63-module corpus (PolyBench, Embench, Sightglass, CoreMark, AssemblyScript, zlib, zstd, QOI and others): compile latency (fresh process, load plus validate plus code generation) and cold execute latency (fresh process, load, compile, instantiate and first export call) as geometric means of per-module medians of 3 runs after 1 warmup, on AMD64 and ARM64.
claimed_speedup: README: 'compile 5x quicker and execute 1.9x faster than wazero' (the README figures are not reproduced in the committed study). Committed bench/runtime-corpus-study.md geometric means on Ryzen 7 7800X3D: compile wall wago 6.42 ms vs wazero 7.83, wasmtime 9.77, V8 14.44, wasmer 14.80 ms; cold execute wago 7.34 ms vs wazero 8.11, wasmtime 7.56, V8 16.84, wasmer 10.88, wasm3 9.91, wasmi 12.34 ms. On Apple M4 Max: compile wago 4.43 ms vs wazero 5.32, wasmtime 7.12, V8 14.75, wasmer 8.91; cold execute wago 4.77 ms vs wazero 5.27, wasmtime 5.95, V8 15.59, wasmer 6.76. So about 1.2x to 3.3x faster compile and 1.03x (wasmtime, AMD64) to 3.3x (V8, ARM64) lower cold execute latency (derived from page data). From the committed JSON, wago's internal Go-side compile time is a geometric mean 0.32x of wazero's over 63 modules (derived).
tradeoffs: Pure-Go Wasm-to-native compiler (amd64 and arm64); beta, WASI and the Component Model are external plugins. Not a steady-state throughput claim.
caveats: Cold-start wall times include process start, so the large wins over V8 and WAVM partly reflect the CLI startup cost of those engines, and wasm3/wasmi/wazero/wazy use different adapters; the execute metric includes compile. Wago's cold execute is within noise of Wasmtime on AMD64 (7.34 vs 7.56 ms). Compute-heavy steady-state speed was not isolated. The README's 5x and 1.9x figures point at wago.sh (blocked) and do not match the committed study. First-party benchmark (harness, JSON and study are public, CPU named, Go version and flags not), so held at C. Version is 0.0.0 beta.

compiler_and_flags: Baselines built as: node run-v8.mjs <case>.js for V8; asc <case>.as.ts -O3 for AssemblyScript; native references clang -O3 -march=native, rustc -C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native; jz compile(src, { optimize: 'speed' }); clang 19.1.6, jz 0.9.2, asc 0.28.19 (results.json meta).
name: jz (dy/jz)
baseline: V8 (Node.js) running the same JavaScript, plus AssemblyScript
workload: Numeric JavaScript kernels (DSP, audio, image, hashing, parsing, simulation; 63 cases, 55 with parity against V8) compiled ahead of time to WebAssembly by jz and run on Node's V8 Wasm engine, versus the same source as raw JS on Node/V8.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Faster than V8 and AssemblyScript on almost every kernel we measure, about 2x on average'. Committed bench/results.json (Apple M4 Max, Node v25.9.0): geometric mean of per-case median time ratios jz/V8 0.443 over 55 checksum-verified cases (about 2.26x faster, faster on 52 of 55); jz/AssemblyScript 0.448 over 50 cases (faster on 44); jz in wasmtime 0.498 of V8 (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Compiles a statically analyzable JavaScript subset: no GC (bump allocator), no eval or Proxy, fixed object shapes, regexes at build time, 32-bit array indices, 64-bit wrapping BigInt. Pre-1.0.
caveats: Compares compiled-to-Wasm code against V8 running the same JS on numeric kernels chosen by the author, with the project's own harness; ratios here are this agent's geometric means from results.json rows with parity 'ok' (the bench page jz.js.org was not opened). V8 loses mostly because of dynamic-typing overhead the subset removes, not because Wasm is a faster VM. The harness records a per-case verdict and notes rows that are only a tie.

name: revm
workload: evm-bench Solidity workloads: erc20 approval-transfer, mint and transfer, snailtracer and ten-thousand-hashes, summed per runner.
claimed_speedup: evm-bench README table, sum of five workloads: revm 84.8 ms, Geth 235 ms, pyrevm 194 ms, py-evm on PyPy 7.201 s, py-evm on CPython 19.0886 s, ethereumjs 146.3218 s; so revm is about 2.8x faster than Geth (derived from page data). evmone, the C++ EVM, is faster still at 66 ms (revm is 1.285x evmone).
stars_or_usage: 2.2k stars; used by Reth, Foundry, Optimism and Risc0
tradeoffs: Rust EVM built as a customizable execution framework (hooks, custom specs), not only an interpreter; it is slower than evmone and the benchmark does not cover its experimental revmc JIT.
caveats: Third-party suite (evm-bench by Ziyad Edher, GPL-3.0, 225 stars) with public code but no CPU, compiler flags or runner versions on the README, and the table is undated, so revm and Geth versions are unknown and may be old. The runners compare different embeddings (Geth runner vs revm runner), so call overhead is part of the numbers. This entry is the revm-versus-Geth evidence; evmone is already catalogued.

name: watr
workload: Compiling test/example/brownian.wat to a Wasm binary 500 times in a loop, in-process (JavaScript builds of each compiler); a second table compares watr's optimizer to wasm-opt over the 21 modules in test/example.
claimed_speedup: README metrics: watr 3,123 op/s versus wabt 859 op/s (about 3.6x, derived from page data), Binaryen 473 op/s (about 6.6x), the WebAssembly spec wast.js 1,509 op/s and wat-compiler 355 op/s. Optimizer table: watr/optimize about 110 ms in-process for the batch versus wasm-opt -Oz 990 ms as a CLI run (about 9x, but includes process spawn), with total output 19,734 B against 19,852 B for -Oz and 22,302 B for -O3.
tradeoffs: Pure-JavaScript, zero-dependency WAT compiler (about 44 KB minified) that also polyfills, minifies and optimizes; no native core, so large modules are slower than Binaryen.
caveats: Benchmark code is public (test/bench.js, browser-run, single brownian.wat input, N=500) but the README gives no CPU, browser or Node version. wabt and Binaryen are measured as their JavaScript/Wasm builds, not as native CLIs; for a 5.5 MB module the README itself says Binaryen's native core is faster (0.44 s versus about 2.6 s optimize plus 0.19 s compile). The 110 ms versus 990 ms optimizer comparison pits an in-process call against a spawned CLI.
found_via: Followed jz's benchmark README (lab case 'watr'), then opened github.com/dy/watr, its readme.md, LICENSE and test/bench.js
